content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed BFNO, an efficient approximation of ODE by neural network. A solution of an ODE is given by an integral of the time-derivative. Alternatively, the proposed method assumes the solution first, and defines the right-hand of the ODE as the derivative of the solution. This is done by using neural operator framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

Some parts of the idea I could understand sound interesting.

## Weakness

It is difficult understand the detailed definition of the proposed method. $g_k$ is a vector, as stated after (8). Then, what does the Fourier transformation $\mathcal F$ applied to the vector $g_k$ in (11) mean? Here, $g_k$ has an argument $x$, so is it now an image or tensor? After (11), it is stated that "$g$ is theoretically a spatial function", but it was defined as an output of a fully-connected network $TimeEnc$ after (8). How a vector $h(t)$ is transformed into a spatial function $g_0$ by a fully-connected layers? According to Appendices C--E, $TimeEnc$ might be a convolutional neural network.

It is unclear to me why the proposed "method provides a more rigorous way for defining the ODE function" (as stated in Section 4.1). It is unclear how the proposed method comes from the idea in (7); what is the component corresponding to the differential operator $D_f$?

Because of the above reason, the problem setting is unclear; it is unclear whether the proposed method is generally applicable to any ODE or specialized to an ODE whose state is an image.

In this manuscript, the authors refer to the right-hand side of ODE as the "ODE function," but this usage is uncommon.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The definitions of the variables and processes are unclear and unreproducible. hence, it is hard to evaluate the novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: Some parts of the idea I could understand sound interesting, but most parts are unclear. If Sections 3 and 4 are properly rewritten, this study could potentially earn a good rating.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper designs a new neural operator structure called the branched Fourier neural operator (BFNO), which is suitable for modeling the ODE function. It shows improved performance for several general machine-learning tasks compared to existing NODE models. The paper links a Fourier transform in the neural ordinary differential equations and shows some superiority. However, the Fourier transform usually needs to satisfy certain boundary conditions and is very expensive to compute, so the application of this method will not be broad.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

This paper expands on the practical applications of neural odes.

The paper makes many comparisons with other methods, and the arguments are solid.

Weaknesses

The title is a bit strange.

Figure 1 is not very clear. Why is the structure of f a network with input h and output h derivatives?

Figure 3 shows that the network does not converge because there are not enough epochs. After convergence, are the errors of BFNO and other networks similar?

How to deal with doing Fourier transform on non-periodic problems?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This method is innovative and reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The article is clearly written. But the results are not very impressive. The methods used for comparison are not good enough. Maybe neural ODE is not suitable for solving this kind of problems

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper combined the ideas of neural ODE (NODE) and Fourier neural operator (FNO), and proposed branched FNO (BFNO)-NODE. Specifically, BFNO (FNO with dynamic global convolutional operation) is used to approximate the ODE function in NODE. Compared to existing NODE models, BFNO-NODE showed better performance for some tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- There are two novelties in the paper: (1) extend FNO to BFNO by using more branches, and (2) use BFNO in NODE.
- BFNO-NODE achieves better accuracy than other NODEs in image classification, time series classification, and image generation.

Weaknesses
- There are two novelties as mentioned above, but they are incremental.
- Theoretically, neural operators (FNO/DeepONet) can approximate any nonlinear operator. In neural operator papers, the main focus is PDE, but there are some ODE cases, such as in https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-021-00302-5. In the paper, the authors showed empirically FNO doesn’t work well, but it is unclear theoretically why FNO doesn’t work here, and why using more branches makes FNO works.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed BFNO-NODE combines FNO and NODE to achieve better accuracy. However, there is lack of understanding why BFNO works.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a modified neural ordinary differential equation where the vector field is modeled by a branched Fourier neural operator. The performance of the model is demonstrated on several tasks showing that it performs well.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Exploring the connections between neural ODEs and neural operators are an interesting idea. However, this paper does not provide any interesting theoretical results that would help to better understand connections between the two research areas. Essentially, this work is modeling the time derivative by some `fancy’ neural network that represents some form of a branched Fourier neural operator. In the absence of theoretical results, this work appears to be incremental.  Further, the experiments are of limited interest. Maybe 2-3 years ago the presented results were of interest to demonstrate that Neural ODEs work. But now I don’t think that these results are of any great interest to the ML community, i.e, to see that a model can improve the test accuracy on CIFAR-10 from 59.5% to 60% ish is not interesting. Also, recent work has demonstrated that ODE-Nets can achieve performance like ResNets [1,2], with less parameters than the model presented here. Similarly, a comparison with state-of-the-art generative models is missing.  

Finally, it is not discussed whether the proposed modification renders a universal approximator? Theory should show that the proposed model can overcome limitations of Neural ODEs. 

[1] ANODEV2: A Coupled Neural ODE Framework (NeurIPS 2019). 

[2] Stateful ODE-Nets using Basis Function Expansions (NeurIPS 2021).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, this paper is of okay quality, but the organization of the paper can be improved. Several parts are redundant. Further, the results can be presented in a more appealing and concise manner. The quality and number of experiments do not meet the standard for an empirical conference paper. Code is provided for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper combines Neural ODEs with ideas from neural operators. This research direction seems plausible and of interest. But this paper does not provide any new interesting insights that help to better understand the connections between the two areas and the benefits that neural ODEs can gain from neural operators. Essentially, this paper is replacing the right-hand side of a neural ODE with a highly parameterized neural network in order to slightly improve the performance. I feel that the ideas presented are of little relevance and the results are not significant enough to accept this paper for publication.
